identity.title: Not All Tokens Are What You Need for Pretraining

problem.claim: Improve language-model pretraining by identifying and emphasizing more useful training tokens.

gap.claim: Prior pretraining methods uniformly applied next-token loss to all tokens, without accounting for token-level differences in training dynamics or importance.

contributions.claim: Analyzes token-level training dynamics and reports distinct loss patterns across tokens.
Introduces Rho-1, which uses Selective Language Modeling: a reference model scores tokens, and training focuses loss on higher-scoring tokens aligned with the desired distribution.
Reports gains from selective-token pretraining on mathematical and general-task settings.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present Rho-1 and Selective Language Modeling as a departure from training on every next token in the corpus.

author_reported_evidence.claim: On continual pretraining with 15B OpenWebMath tokens, Rho-1 reportedly improved few-shot accuracy by up to 30% absolute across nine math tasks.
After fine-tuning, Rho-1-1B and Rho-1-7B reportedly reached 40.6% and 51.8% on MATH, matching DeepSeekMath while using 3% of the pretraining tokens.
With 80B general tokens, Rho-1 reportedly improved average performance by 6.8% across 15 diverse tasks.

narrative_sequence.summary: Existing methods apply next-token loss uniformly; the authors posit that token importance differs.
Token-level training dynamics show distinct loss patterns for different tokens.
These observations motivate Rho-1 and its reference-model-scored Selective Language Modeling procedure.
The abstract reports improvements on math tasks, MATH, and diverse general tasks under continual pretraining and fine-tuning.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links a token-dynamics analysis to a selective-training mechanism that scores tokens with a reference model and concentrates loss on higher-scoring tokens.

lessons.interpretation: A paper can make a method rationale more traceable by connecting an observed training pattern to a specific design choice.
lessons.application: When proposing data or loss selection, first report the unit-level diagnostic, then state how its signal determines selection and objective weighting.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the selection signal is not measurable before training or when uniform coverage is essential to the task.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the reference model, score definition, selection fraction, training schedule, baselines, or variance across runs.
The reported MATH comparison and token-efficiency claim lack detailed evaluation and token-count context in the abstract.
